faq.q: What are the three squares on a QR code for?
faq.a: They are finder patterns. Their special nested-square shape is easy to spot from any direction, so the phone can find the code, work out which way up it is and correct for tilt.
asks: Why do QR codes have squares in the corners?

faq.q: How does a QR code store information?
faq.a: Each tiny square, called a module, is a bit: dark for 1 and light for 0. The bits are grouped into bytes that spell out a web address, text or other data, plus error-correction bytes.
asks: What do the dots in a QR code mean?

faq.a: Extra bytes are calculated from the message using Reed–Solomon coding and stored in the code too. If some bytes are unreadable, the maths can work out what they must have been.
asks: How do QR codes fix mistakes?

faq.q: How much of a QR code can be damaged?
faq.a: It depends on the error-correction level chosen: about 7, 15, 25 or 30 percent of the data can be restored. That is why some QR codes still scan with a logo in the middle.
asks: Why can QR codes have a logo in the middle?

faq.a: Masahiro Hara and his team at the Japanese company Denso Wave invented QR codes in 1994 to track car parts in factories. QR stands for quick response.

facts: QR codes were invented in 1994 by Denso Wave, a Toyota group company, to track car parts.
QR codes have four error-correction levels, L, M, Q and H, restoring about 7, 15, 25 and 30 percent of the data.

quiz.say: A QR code on a poster has a muddy smear across one corner, yet it still scans. Why?
quiz.show: A smeared QR code still works because…

options.show: Error-correction data rebuilds the missing part
options.say: Error-correction data rebuilds the missing part

quiz.why: Extra Reed–Solomon data in the code lets the software calculate the hidden bits.

wrong.1: The phone does not guess; it recovers the exact data with maths.
wrong.2: Cameras can see the mud; the code works despite it.
